title: System Design & Scalability
description: The distributed-systems knowledge senior interviews probe and production work demands — caching, sharding, consistency, queues, resilience patterns and the tradeoffs behind each.

steps.title: What system design interviews actually test
steps.description: Requirements gathering, estimation, high-level design, deep dives and tradeoff discussion. Learn the shape of the conversation before the components.

steps.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
steps.description: Latency numbers every engineer should know, QPS, storage and bandwidth maths. Estimation turns vague designs into concrete, defensible ones.

steps.title: Client-server and the request path
steps.description: DNS resolution, TCP and TLS handshakes, HTTP semantics and keep-alive. Trace one request end to end before designing systems of them.

steps.title: API design
steps.description: REST resource modelling, status codes, idempotency, pagination and versioning, plus where GraphQL and gRPC fit better.

steps.title: Relational databases in depth
steps.description: ACID, isolation levels, locking, MVCC and transaction anomalies. Most data bugs at scale are isolation-level misunderstandings.

steps.title: Indexing and query planning
steps.description: B-trees, composite indexes, covering indexes and reading query plans. The difference between a fast and unusable system is often one index.

steps.title: NoSQL data models
steps.description: Key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores, and the access patterns each is genuinely good at. Model for queries, not for entities.

steps.title: Replication
steps.description: Leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication, replication lag and read-your-writes consistency. The source of most surprising bugs.

steps.title: Partitioning and sharding
steps.description: Range versus hash partitioning, hot spots, rebalancing and the pain of resharding a live system. Choose a shard key you can live with for years.

steps.title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
steps.description: Strong, eventual and causal consistency, and what you truly give up during a partition. Get past the slogan into the actual tradeoffs.

steps.title: Caching strategies
steps.description: Cache-aside, read-through and write-behind, TTLs, eviction policies, stampedes and invalidation — the genuinely hard part.

steps.title: Content delivery networks
steps.description: Edge caching, cache keys, purging and origin shielding. Often the single cheapest latency win available.

steps.title: Load balancing
steps.description: L4 versus L7, round-robin, least-connections and consistent hashing, plus health checks and connection draining.

steps.title: Message queues and event streaming
steps.description: Queues versus logs, consumer groups, ordering, delivery guarantees and dead-letter handling with Kafka, RabbitMQ or SQS.

steps.title: Asynchronous processing
steps.description: Background jobs, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, scheduling and idempotent consumers. Anything slow belongs off the request path.

steps.title: Idempotency and exactly-once delivery
steps.description: Idempotency keys, deduplication and the outbox pattern. Understand why exactly-once delivery is a myth and exactly-once processing is not.

steps.title: Monolith, services and microservices
steps.description: Service boundaries, coupling, distributed transactions and when a monolith is the correct senior answer. Complexity must be earned.

steps.title: Saga pattern and distributed transactions
steps.description: Choreography versus orchestration, compensating actions and eventual consistency across services once two-phase commit is off the table.

steps.title: Resilience patterns
steps.description: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation. Design assuming every dependency will fail, because it will.

steps.title: Rate limiting and backpressure
steps.description: Token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding windows, plus shedding load before a system collapses under it.

steps.title: Consensus and coordination
steps.description: Leader election, distributed locks, quorums and Raft. Know enough to avoid implementing consensus yourself.

steps.title: Search systems
steps.description: Inverted indexes, tokenisation, relevance ranking and near-real-time indexing with Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

steps.title: Object storage and file handling
steps.description: Blob stores, presigned uploads, chunking and multi-region durability. Never proxy large files through your application servers.

steps.title: Observability
steps.description: Structured logs, RED and USE metrics, distributed tracing and SLIs, SLOs and error budgets. You cannot operate what you cannot see.

steps.title: Capacity planning and load testing
steps.description: Model growth, find the knee in the curve with load tests, and plan headroom before traffic finds the limit for you.

steps.title: Security in system design
steps.description: Authentication and authorisation between services, secrets management, encryption in transit and at rest, and multi-tenant isolation.

steps.title: Deployment and release safety
steps.description: Blue-green and canary releases, feature flags and safe database migrations with backwards-compatible schema changes.

steps.title: Case study: URL shortener
steps.description: Key generation, storage choice, read-heavy caching, custom aliases and analytics. The classic warm-up that exercises real tradeoffs.

steps.title: Case study: news feed
steps.description: Fan-out on write versus read, ranking, the celebrity problem and pagination over a changing timeline.

steps.title: Case study: chat and real-time systems
steps.description: WebSockets, presence, message ordering, delivery receipts and offline sync across devices.

steps.title: Case study: rate-limited public API
steps.description: Multi-tenant quotas, distributed counters, fair queuing and abuse protection at the edge.

steps.title: Mock interviews and writing designs down
steps.description: Practise aloud under time, and write architecture decision records. Communicating a design is scored as heavily as the design itself.
